blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely from scratch. We ask whether a pretrained video generator can instead provide the prior for both inverse and forward dynamics. We introduce O$^{2}$LaF, built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize both models from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them to their distinct roles: a feed-forward transition encoder with learnable action queries for inverse dynamics, and a causal, action-conditioned video generator for forward dynamics. By controlling information access and optimizing both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck, O$^{2}$LaF learns transferable actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, O$^{2}$LaF sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing and enables stronger zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments. Beyond generative video priors, we further extend our framework to predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, achieving competitive performance. Our findings suggest a broader paradigm for latent-action learning: repurposing pretrained video models to discover transferable actions and predict their consequences.

Existing methods differ in where pretrained priors enter this pipeline
(Fig. 2 ), leaving a gap on each side.
On the inverse side, IDMs are learned from scratch, either on raw
pixels [ 85 , 8 , 20 ] or on top of frozen pretrained
features [ 9 , 21 , 54 ] .
They must learn to infer actions from transitions largely through the FDM’s
reconstruction supervision, and such specialized latent action models are
outperformed by general visual foundation models [ 54 ] .
Olaf-World [ 35 ] aligns latent actions with an external video
representation to improve transferability, but its IDM is still learned from scratch.
On the forward side, recent methods adopt a pretrained video generator as the
FDM [ 62 , 76 ] , whose initial-frame
conditioning supplies appearance, reducing its leakage into the latent actions.
However, they keep the standard diffusion recipe, under which the generator can learn
to disregard the latent action [ 76 ] , underusing its prior as a learning signal.
Yet modern video Diffusion Transformers (video DiTs) [ 58 ] are pretrained at scale to model how visual states evolve over time [ 82 , 59 , 41 , 71 , 70 , 7 , 50 ] .
Their representations encode rich temporal structure, while their generative
dynamics learn to predict complex visual changes.
Much of the prior needed for latent action learning therefore already
exists inside a pretrained video generator.
This raises a simple question: can a pretrained video DiT serve both inverse and forward dynamics for
latent action learning? Doing so is nontrivial: the two dynamics place different demands on the same video
prior, requiring careful control over what each can access.

blocks.en:
We introduce O 2 LaF , a self-supervised latent-action framework
built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics .
We initialize the IDM and FDM from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them independently for their respective roles.
For inverse dynamics , we repurpose the video DiT as a feed-forward transition encoder, where action queries extract one compact latent action per visual transition under causal temporal attention.
For forward dynamics , we retain the generative role of the video DiT and introduce causal joint prediction, which predicts the future state sequence jointly, conditioned on the inferred latent actions, while preserving temporal causality.
Unlike visual synthesis, where training often emphasizes intermediate-noise timesteps [ 18 , 51 ] , the FDM here also provides the learning signal that shapes the latent-action space.
At these partially noisy timesteps, the noisy future still reveals much of the target, allowing the FDM to predict the future with little reliance on the latent action.
We therefore train at high noise, which suppresses this target leakage and forces the FDM to depend on the inferred action.
The two dynamics are optimized end-to-end through a compact continuous latent-action space.

We further systematically study how the two dynamics shape the learned action space.
For example, causal joint prediction outperforms autoregressive prediction by removing clean-history shortcuts, while role-specific noise levels reveal distinct information requirements for the two dynamics.
Beyond generative video priors, we also extend the repurposing principle to self-supervised predictive representation models [ 2 ] and language-supervised video multimodal models [ 43 ] as alternative IDM backbones.

does not necessarily translate into better downstream
generative control, highlighting the importance of
validating latent actions beyond probing through

blocks.en:
We evaluate O 2 LaF across camera navigation and robotic manipulation.
It sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing across both discrete and continuous action spaces, indicating stronger alignment with ground-truth actions.
Beyond probing, the learned actions also transfer without target adaptation, enabling zero-shot control across first- and third-person navigation and human-to-robot transfer in manipulation.
The causal FDM readily serves as a video world model, while its learned action-conditioned dynamics provide a strong initialization for higher-fidelity two-stage deployment.
Our contributions are threefold: • We introduce O 2 LaF , a self-supervised latent-action framework
that repurposes a pretrained video DiT into end-to-end trained inverse and
forward dynamics models. • Through a systematic study, we show that latent-action learning depends
critically on how the two dynamics are factorized and what information they receive. • O 2 LaF achieves state-of-the-art few-shot action probing across camera navigation and robotic manipulation, while demonstrating strong zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments and reusable action-conditioned dynamics for world modeling.

blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en: 2.1 Latent Action Learning from Videos
blocks.zh: 2.1 从视频中学习慢动作

blocks.en:
Latent action learning turns large-scale action-unlabeled video into a reusable intermediate control representation.
The same representation can be consumed by a world model to control future visual evolution [ 8 , 20 , 35 , 21 , 19 ] , or produced by a policy or planner as a surrogate for physical actions [ 66 , 85 , 9 , 14 , 15 , 83 ] .
Recent work further seeks to make this control space transferable across contexts and embodiments [ 35 , 31 , 4 , 37 ] .

最近的工作进一步力求使这种控制空间在上下文和表象上可以转让[35、31、4、37]。

blocks.en:
Existing methods differ in where pretrained priors enter the
inverse–forward dynamics pipeline (Fig. 2 ).
Early approaches learn both transition inference and prediction directly from the target videos [ 66 , 8 , 85 , 20 ] .
To reduce shortcuts from raw-pixel reconstruction, later methods move the prediction target into pretrained semantic feature spaces, emphasizing motion and task-relevant change over appearance details [ 15 , 9 , 74 ] .
A related direction strengthens the forward model with pretrained video priors, reducing appearance burden or replacing the from-scratch FDM [ 62 , 76 , 48 ] .
Pretrained video representations have also been used as external temporal supervision to orient latent actions across visual contexts [ 35 ] .

blocks.en: 5.4 Balancing Action Learning and Generation
blocks.zh: 5.4 平衡行动学习和一代

blocks.en:
Jointly learning latent actions and a generative
video world model is a compelling objective [ 76 ] .
Yet the FDM faces a practical trade-off: learning informative
actions requires limiting visual shortcuts, whereas
high-fidelity generation benefits from broader noise coverage.
In O 2 LaF, causal prediction and high-noise supervision
serve the former objective, but compromise the latter.
We investigate whether both objectives can be reconciled
within end-to-end training.

然而,发展筹资面临着一个实际的权衡:学习信息
动作需要限制视觉快捷键,而
高纯度的生成得益于更广泛的噪音覆盖。
O 2 LaF中,因果预测和高噪音监督
服务于前一个目标,但损害后一个目标。
我们调查两个目标能否调和
在端对端训练中。

We first study FDM noise sampling and IDM gradient routing.

Given the inherent tension, we adopt a two-stage approach [ 35 ] , freezing the learned
IDM and training a bidirectional FDM.
This substantially improves generation quality.
Moreover, initializing from the jointly trained FDM,
rather than the original pretrained video DiT,
further improves both visual quality and action-following
fidelity.

blocks.en: 6 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 6 结论

blocks.en:
We presented O 2 LaF, a self-supervised framework
that repurposes a pretrained video DiT for both inverse
and forward dynamics.
By tailoring the two dynamics to their distinct roles
and controlling information access, O 2 LaF learns
transferable latent actions from unlabeled videos.
Across navigation and robotic manipulation, it achieves
state-of-the-art few-shot action probing and enables
zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and
human–robot embodiments.
These findings establish pretrained video generators
as reusable dynamics priors for action discovery
and controllable world modeling.

blocks.en: C.2 FDM as a Policy Verifier
blocks.zh: C.2 作为政策验证人的FDM

blocks.en:
Frontier AI models are quickly becoming capable robot agents:
they write robot policies as code [ 44 ] and control a two-armed robot from camera images in simulation [ 1 ] .
Such agents are increasingly built and tested in simulators,
but a simulator only approximates the real scene, and real-robot trials are slow and costly [ 91 ] ,
so a behavior that succeeds in simulation may still fail on the robot.
Our FDM offers a cheap check across this gap:
starting from a real photo, it predicts what a candidate action sequence will do in the real scene,
before the robot executes it.

前沿AI模型正在迅速成为有能力的机器人代理:
他们将机器人政策写成代码[44],并在模拟[1]中从相机图像中控制一个双臂机器人.
这种药剂越来越多地在模拟器中制造和测试,

从一个真实的照片开始, 它预测一个候选动作序列 将在真实的场景,
在机器人执行之前

blocks.en:
For each scene, Opus 5.5 (high) rebuilds a MuJoCo [ 73 ] simulation from the robot’s head-camera photo, using the GR-1 model from robosuite [ 92 ] .
We then script candidate grasps and run them in physics as a reference.
To query the FDM, we render each trajectory with all movable objects removed, so the latent actions the IDM extracts describe the robot’s motion but not the simulated outcome, and roll them out from the real photo.
When the two agree (Fig. 12 a,b), the FDM reproduces both a successful placement and a failed grasp, while keeping details the rebuild simplifies, such as the real pan.
When they disagree (Fig. 12 c), the simulator lifts a salt shaker that, in the FDM rollout, stays on the table.
The rebuilt scene suggests a cause: the small tapered glass shakers with metal caps become taller plain cylinders, and the glass vase beside them becomes an opaque cylinder, so a grasp that fits the rebuilt shaker may miss the real one.
Without executing the trajectory we cannot tell which prediction is right, but such a disagreement flags an action worth checking before it reaches the robot.
We see this pre-execution check as a promising direction for future work.

为了查询FDM,我们使每个轨迹都与所有可移动的物体一起被移除,所以IDM提取出来的潜伏动作描述了机器人的运动,而不是模拟的结果,然后从真实的照片中推出。
当两者同意时(图12 a,b),FDM同时复制一个成功的放置和一个失败的抓取,同时保留细节重建简化,如真锅.
当他们不同意(图12c)时,模拟器会举起一个盐摇杆,在FDM推出时,它会留在桌上.
重建的场景暗示了一个原因:带有金属帽的小带状玻璃摇摆器变成更高的平坦的圆筒,旁边的玻璃花瓶变成一个不透明的圆筒,因此一个与重建的摇摆器相匹配的抓住器可能会错过真正的圆筒.
不执行轨迹,我们无法分辨哪个预测是正确的, 但这种分歧标志着一个值得检查的行动,在它到达机器人之前。
我们认为,这种预先执行检查是未来工作的有希望的方向。

Structure and interpretability of latent actions. Although our learned actions transfer across visual
contexts and embodiments, their underlying structure
remains poorly understood.
Beyond quantitative probing, interpreting individual latent actions still largely relies on inspecting their corresponding reference videos.
Learning more interpretable, compositional, and appearance-invariant action representations remains an important direction for future work.

blocks.en:
Toward decision-making world models. O 2 LaF learns latent actions that explain visual transitions and control future video generation.
However, its dynamics are optimized for visual prediction rather than decision-making.
Unlike compact dynamics models that support efficient imagined rollouts and policy optimization [ 25 , 45 ] , video diffusion models incur substantial computational costs and do not directly expose executable actions or task-relevant rewards.
Bridging video-derived action representations with
efficient, decision-relevant dynamics is an important
direction toward planning and closed-loop control.
